mentions.name: Hessra
mentions.description: An authentication platform offering new identity primitives and capability-style tokens built on biscuits. It is being extended with integrations that add an extremely fine-grained access control layer in front of systems that lack it, such as backend-for-frontend (BFF) systems, brownfield applications with poor auth, and OAuth setups limited to coarse scopes.
mentions.problem: Many systems lack fine-grained access control: BFF systems, legacy brownfield apps with poor auth, and OAuth implementations that only support coarse scopes.
mentions.source_excerpt:
I'm working on https://www.hessra.net/

We've built a new auth platform with some new identity primitives and capability-style tokens using biscuits.

Right now, I'm trying to figure out ways to apply it and am looking into offering integrations with extremely fine-grained access control that wouldn't have it otherwise. So adding a fine-grained access layer in front of stuff like backend-for-frontend (BFF) systems, brownfield stuff with poor auth, or even OAuth stuff that just have really coarse scopes.

mentions.name: Hessra
mentions.description: An authorization system based on the Biscuit token format (decentralized, signed, and attenuable) that gives every machine-to-machine request its own embedded, verifiable authorization logic in a small capability token. Tokens can be delegated, restricted, and verified locally with no extra network calls after issuance, and support features like multiple parties signing off before a token is valid or requiring a series of micro-services to sign a token. Its early use case is replacing API keys with identity tokens that expire, delegate, and prove possession, enabling step-up to fine-grained authorization.
mentions.problem: JWTs, Zanzibar-style policy engines, and API keys lack per-request embedded, verifiable authorization logic and easy delegation, restriction, and possession proof.
mentions.source_excerpt: Building https://www.hessra.net/, an authorization system based on the Biscuit token format (decentralized, signed, and attenuable). The goal is to push beyond JWTs and Zanzibar-style policy engines by giving every machine-to-machine request its own embedded, verifiable authorization logic in a small capability token.

mentions.name: Hessra
mentions.description: An identity and authorization service built around Biscuit tokens instead of JWTs, aiming to decompose auth primitives so they are easier to use in service-to-service cases. Shipped features include an offline-delegatable identity token enabling an API key model without maintaining a token database (with hashing/expiry encoded in the token and upgrade paths via authorization tokens and customer delegation). It also explores higher-order authorization flows such as service chains, where each hop (edge → app → DB) adds attestations, and multi-party authorization requiring two independent services/orgs to co-sign an authorization token for cross-org or on-prem deployments. An OAuth 2.1 profile is in progress, mapping the identity token to a refresh token and the authorization token to an access token.
mentions.problem: JWTs feel like problems waiting to happen, and OAuth is clunky in practice; Biscuit tokens are claimed to provide stronger guarantees and be harder to get wrong.
mentions.audience: Service-to-service and API developers; people building auth systems
mentions.source_excerpt: I’m working on https://www.hessra.net/, an identity + authorization service built around [Biscuits](https://www.biscuitsec.org/) instead of JWTs. The goal is to decompose auth primitives so they’re easier to use in service-to-service cases, while also showing off what Biscuit tokens make possible.
